title: The Medicare Prescription Drug Improvement and Modernization Act: prescription drugs and academic medicine.
source_type: Academic medicine : journal of the Association of American Medical Colleges
text_summary: 本文评析2003年《Medicare处方药改进与现代化法案》（MMA）首次向老年和残障Medicare受益人普遍提供处方药保障后的制度设计及其对学术医学的影响。文章重点讨论“甜甜圈缺口”导致的阶段性全额自付、私人计划竞争和药品目录管理带来的选择复杂性与风险选择，以及项目长期成本的不确定性。法案显著减少了无药物保障人数，但低收入双重资格者的转换混乱、慢性病患者负担和私人计划管理仍有隐忧；若药费超支，还可能挤压医院与医师报销。MMA同时借助质量报告、绩效支付和院外住院医培训激励，将资源从高成本急性住院照护转向门诊和预防。作者呼吁学术医学加强政策与处方使用研究，并训练医师成为患者合理用药的有效代理和倡导者。

Health Policy
The Medicare Prescription Drug Improvement
and Modernization Act: Prescription Drugs
and Academic Medicine
Stanley K. Frencher, Jr., MD, MPH, and Sherry Glied, PhD
Abstract
The Medicare Prescription Drug,
Improvement, and Modernization Act
(MMA) provides universally available
prescription drug benefits to elderly and
disabled Medicare beneficiaries for the
first time. This paper first discusses three
controversial features of this legislation:
(1) the form of the prescription drug
benefit package; (2) the use of
competing private plans; and (3) the
uncertainty about the future cost of the
new prescription drug benefit. The paper
then evaluates the implications for
academic medicine of the prescription
drug benefit and other MMA legislative
provisions aimed at improving the quality
of medical practice and shifting away
from acute care. Ultimately, the health of
seniors and the efficient use of public
funds in the new prescription drug
benefit depend centrally on the
prescribing practices of physicians.
Academic medicine should turn its
attention to training the next generation
of physicians to be more effective agents
and advocates for their patients in their
use of pharmaceuticals.
Acad Med. 2006; 81:812–816.
The Medicare Prescription Drug,
Improvement, and Modernization Act
(MMA), which passed in December 2003,
is the most important innovation in the
program’s 40-year existence. The
legislation, although clearly the
complicated, illogical, product of a
contentious political process—a horse
designed by committee—provides
universally available pharmaceutical
insurance to elderly and disabled
Medicare beneficiaries for the first time.
1
The MMA also includes a host of other
provisions, several with direct
implications for academic medicine.
The MMA’s Prescription Drug
Benefit
Before the passage of the MMA, seniors
acquired their prescription drugs in a
variety of ways. Some Medicare
beneficiaries enjoyed employer-
sponsored supplemental retirement
coverage or simply paid out-of-pocket in
order to acquire prescription drugs.
Others obtain supplemental coverage to
Medicare, either by purchasing Medigap
insurance or by receiving “wrap-around”
Medicaid coverage as low-income “dual
eligibles.” (For a guide to terms related to
Medicare, please see List 1.)
The financial and logistical burden for
seniors as a group was inarguable. Seniors
aged 65 years and older consume 30% of
the nation’s prescription drugs and, pre-
MMA, the average senior doled out over
$500 annually or over 3% of his/her
income for prescription drugs.
2
Moreover, the distribution of this burden
among seniors was highly uneven.
Although many well-insured seniors
spent very little on prescription
medications, for the 10% of seniors with
the highest spending, average expenses
exceeded $300 per month.
3 A 2003
nationwide survey found that particularly
vulnerable seniors, including those
without prescription drug coverage, low-
income adults, and the chronically ill,
were much more likely than other seniors
to pay more than $100 monthly for
medications or to forego drug therapy.
3
Under the MMA legislation, seniors with
incomes below 150% of the federal
poverty line, which for 2005 was $9,367
for a single senior, will have access to
prescription drug coverage at no cost.
4,5
Higher-income seniors may elect to
purchase coverage at an estimated
average cost of $37 per month, for a plan
with a $250 deductible and varying out-
of-pocket costs capped at $3,600.
6 Dual
eligibles or Medicare beneficiaries who
had been receiving prescription drug
benefits through a state prescription drug
assistance program will have this existing
coverage replaced by the MMA’s
prescription drug benefit.
Controversial Features of the
MMA’s Prescription Drug Benefit
Three features of this legislation have
generated substantial controversy: (1) the
form of the prescription drug benefit
package; (2) the use of competing private
plans; and (3) the uncertainty about the
future cost of the new prescription drug
benefit. Below, we discuss these three
issues and consider the implications of
the legislation for academic medicine.
Benefit design: The “donut hole”
The MMA’s prescription drug benefit
was designed backward to fit a price tag.
Under a fiscal year (FY) 2004 resolution,
Congress reserved $400 billion over ten
years to pay for a prescription drug
benefit.
6,7 These funds would not have
sufficed to pay for a comprehensive
benefit, given current drug prices and
consumption patterns, so Congress had
to devise a prescription drug benefit to fit
the allotted budget. One option would
have been to provide coverage with
minimal cost-sharing, limiting annual
benefits to a specified cap. This “front-
end” design was common in existing
Medicare Advantage plans (MA-PDs).
8 A
front-end option would be politically
attractive because almost all seniors
would see some costs paid by the new
benefit. This limited benefit design,
however, would have done little to help

those seniors with the greatest
medication expenditures. Targeting
funds broadly would have provided the
least protection to those with the most
need.
A second option would have been to limit
coverage only to those with catastrophic
pharmaceutical expenses, measured
either as expenditures above a specified
dollar level or expenditures in excess of a
specified share of income. Although
catastrophic insurance coverage has the
greatest value from an economic
perspective, offering protection from true
financial risk, this option was politically
unpalatable. Seniors would be paying
premiums for the benefit, but only a
small minority would see tangible
benefits.
The solution to this conundrum was the
prescription drug benefit’s “donut hole”
design. After a $250 deductible, seniors
can buy their first $2,000 of prescription
drugs with only a 25% copayment
(equivalent to $750 out-of-pocket
expense).
9 If they incur more than $5,100
worth of medication expenditures (or
$3,600 out-of-pocket expense), further
spending requires only a 5% copayment.
Expenses between $2,251 and $5,100 —
those in the donut hole—must be paid
100% out-of-pocket.
9 This design, with
fairly high front-end copayments, should
help contain costs. Considerable evidence
suggests that the use of copayments helps
to control prescription drug costs. For
instance, a 1984 study of relatively low
copayments issued to Medicaid recipients
in South Carolina showed decreased
utilization (a portion of which is assumed
to be unnecessary) and reduced
expenditures.
10 Some researchers argue,
however, that this design may not be the
most appropriate prescription drug
financing structure for patients suffering
from chronic disease in need of indefinite
therapy.
11 These patients will typically
find themselves in the “hole,” facing
100% of the cost of their medication.
Prior research shows that “approximately
one-third of beneficiaries with common
chronic diseases did not fill prescriptions
or used less medication than prescribed
because of the out-of-pocket costs they
incurred under a small supplemental
drug benefit.”
11
The influential role of private plans
The second strategic issue faced by the
designers of the MMA’s prescription
drug benefit was how to contain the costs
of the program. In most other countries
that have national prescription drug
benefit programs, the government
directly controls the prices of
pharmaceuticals.
12,13 In some instances,
price control is accomplished through
negotiation with pharmaceutical
companies around their participation in a
national drug list or formulary, which is
the method used by most health
maintenance organizations (HMOs) and,
with considerable success, by the U.S.
Veterans Administration.
13 In other
cases, governments use a reference price
system, reimbursing pharmaceutical
companies based on the prices paid by
other national purchasers, which is the
method used by the Medicaid program.
The United States is the largest
pharmaceutical market in the world,
accounting for over 46% of global
pharmaceutical sales in 2001.
14 Seniors
comprise the largest single group of
purchasers within that market,
accounting for more than one third of
U.S. drug spending and 41% of
outpatient prescription drug
expenses.
14,15 This economic dominance
made a reference pricing system
impractical. Likewise, the size and
importance of the Medicare market led to
concerns about the possibility that under
a formulary system, the government
would have effective veto power over the
introduction of specific drugs.
9,16
The government eschewed the option of
establishing a pharmaceutical price
setting system akin to the system used to
set physician payment rates. Instead, the
legislation turned the administration of
the prescription drug benefit over to
competing, risk-bearing private plans.
These private plans may be stand-alone
drug plans that complement the existing
List 1
Definition of Key Terms Related to Medicare
• Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS)
United States federal agency (formerly known as the Health Care Financing Administration,
HCFA) embedded within the Department of Health and Human Services charged with
administering Medicare, Medicaid, and State Child Health Insurance Program (SCHIP).
• Dual eligibles
Low-income Medicare beneficiaries who had been receiving additional health care benefits
through the Medicaid program including prescription drug coverage and payment of the
Medicare premium.
• Fallback plans
Prescription drug plans that would be established in PDP regions that would otherwise include
fewer than two separate PDP plans offered by different insurance carriers. In these regions,
CMS would contract directly with private insurers, who would administer a prescription drug
plan but would bear very little financial risk for plan performance. (Due to the number of plans
being offered currently, CMS has not called for bids from private companies to provide these
plans.)
• Formularies
Lists of medications approved by states, providers or health plans that can be prescribed
without separate justification or additional authorization. Formularies may be used to
standardize prescribing practices of individual providers and control costs.
• Medicare advantage plans (MA-PDs)
A Medicare beneficiary option that combines coverage for both hospital and ambulatory
services through contracts to private insurance companies or Health Maintenance
Organizations (HMOs) for Medicare beneficiaries (previously referred to as Medicare Plus
Choice).
• Medicaid program
A state-administered health insurance program established under the Social Security Act
designed for low-income individuals and families who fit into certain eligibility groups based on
a number of criteria including but not limited to income, assets, age, pregnancy, or
immigration status. Both federal and state governments contribute toward the costs to a
varying degree state-by-state.
• Medigap
Supplemental health insurance plans offered by private insurance companies that pay for selected
Medicare expenses (e.g., costs of extended stays in the hospitals beyond 60 days; additional days
needed in skilled nursing facility or for at-home recovery following a hospital stay) and provides
beneficiaries with coverage for services otherwise disallowed under Medicare such as
prescription drugs prior to the enactment of the MMA prescription drug plan.

Medicare payment system for physicians
and hospitals or comprehensive Medicare
Advantage plans, which substitute fully
for traditional Medicare. The private
plans may establish their own
formularies, negotiate prices with
pharmaceutical companies, and use
pharmaceutical utilization management
processes (including varying coinsurance
rates) to contain costs.
Congress, in an attempt to promote
competition amongst the private plans,
divided the nation into 34 prescription
drug plan (PDP) regions. The MMA also
required that there be sufficient numbers
of plans within each region to insure
adequate choice for members amongst
other goals. In PDP regions without at
least two risk-bearing private plans, the
government would contract with
“fallback plans,” which would manage
the prescription drug benefit on the
government’s behalf but would face only
limited risk.
17 To date, all PDP regions
have offered multiple plans, so fallback
arrangements have been implemented.
Private risk-bearing plans are permitted
to design their own formularies, but are
required by the legislation to include at
least two drugs from each of a series of
therapeutic classes defined by the
Secretary of Health and Human Services.
The list of therapeutic classes developed
is quite comprehensive, but formulary
choices of private plans may nonetheless
disadvantage beneficiaries who require
costly drugs.
8 Private plans may try to
make formulary choices that deliberately
discourage enrollment among the sickest
beneficiaries, competing instead to attract
the healthiest seniors within the Medicare
population. Although the legislation
prohibits such selection behavior,
enforcement of the prohibition is likely to
be difficult. Strategic competition of this
type could leave those most in need of a
comprehensive benefit without attractive
options, and would ultimately raise costs
to the Medicare program itself.
18
A proliferation of prescription drug plan
options within each PDP region could
create problems for Medicare
beneficiaries who are required to choose
a plan. In the initial round of plan
offerings, which began in March 2005,
some PDP regions offered as many as
2,743 private plans comprised of 1,429
PDPs and 1,314 Medicare Advantage
Prescription Drug plans.
9 Several critics
of the MMA focus on the disparity
between “complexity”’ of the new plan
options and the health literacy of the
elderly population.
18 Beneficiaries in
most regions have the opportunity to
choose between a variety of plan offerings
including HMOs, Participating Provider
Options (PPOs), remaining traditional
fee-for-service, or employer retirement
coverage supplemented by a federally
qualifying prescription drug plan. The
existence of many options, often with
hard-to-follow differences amongst them,
could lead some seniors to forego making
a choice altogether. Choosing a plan
could be particularly difficult for the
roughly 25% of beneficiaries who suffer
from a cognitive impairment.
19
Advocates have also expressed concern
about private plans using “pharmacy
utilization management” techniques,
such as multitiered formularies with
copayments that vary by category of drug
chosen.
20 Research on the use of these
techniques in the under-65 population
suggests that many people fail to switch
to lower-cost drugs when higher
copayments are introduced. A substantial
share (21% in some studies) stop taking
their medications altogether, whereas
others pay higher copayments rather than
making a switch to a lower-cost drug.
21,22
None of these issues, however, concern
the 45% of Medicare beneficiaries who
lacked coverage altogether for at least
part of the year before the legislation was
implemented.
19 These beneficiaries are
clearly better off with the new
prescription drug benefit offered by the
MMA. For the population with existing
privately purchased (or employer-
provided coverage), the options of plans
offered under the new prescription drug
benefit may or may not be better than the
coverage it replaced. The most difficult
problems are likely to arise around the
dual eligibles who had been obtaining
pharmaceutical coverage through the
Medicaid program. This population,
which includes a preponderance of
disabled and very ill beneficiaries, will
move from public prescription drug
benefits programs designed around their
needs to private plans that are likely to
find serving this population relatively
unattractive.
In practice, the effects of these various
risks in the early phase of the program
appear to have been real but modest. By
May 2006, of the 43 million seniors
eligible for prescription drug benefits,
more than 31.1 million were enrolled in
MMA plans. About 8.1 million of this
group had voluntarily selected a PDP or
MA plan through the MMA. About 4
million held coverage through continuing
participation in an existing MA plan.
Another 6.4 million had been
autoenrolled in a plan because they had
previously held Medicaid drug coverage
as dual eligibles. In addition to these 31.1
million people, an estimated 5.8 million
others continued to hold comparable
alternative drug coverage as retirees,
leaving only about 7.2 million Medicare
beneficiaries without drug coverage, 3.6
million fewer than had lacked coverage
before the MMA.
23
As advocates had feared, however, the
transition to MMA coverage for the dual
eligible group has often been rocky. Dual
eligibles, who expected to seamlessly
transition into the new prescription drug
benefit, faced inappropriate cost-sharing
charges; untimely and inaccurate
information from CMS officials;
inefficient appeals and exceptions
processes. Worst of all, some dual
eligibles arrives at pharmacies only to
find out they were not enrolled at all.
24 In
the first few months of the program,
several states have continued to pay for
dual eligible drug coverage while the
problems in the system are worked out.
24
The future cost of the MMA?
Almost immediately after Congress
passed the MMA, the government’s chief
actuary released estimates suggesting that
the prescription drug benefit would be
substantially more costly than had
previously been forecasted. The
Congressional Budget Office changed its
own budgetary projections by nearly $41
billion before the act had even been fully
enacted.
25 Many components of these
cost estimates are highly uncertain. 26
There have been few studies examining
the effect of a new prescription drug
benefit on the level of utilization of
pharmaceuticals.
27 No one knows how
successful the new private plans will be in
controlling Medicare prices or
utilization— or how many beneficiaries
will choose to participate in them. In this
respect, the early stages of the program
have been encouraging, with the average
premium of MMA coverage purchased by
seniors well below the $37 initially
estimated by CMS.
28 However, the ability
Health Policy
Academic Medicine, Vol. 81, No. 9 / September 2006814

 

of the plans to maintain cost control and
the future path, and costs, of drug
innovation are inherently unknown.
The cost of the prescription drug benefit
may prove more difficult for Medicare to
control than either hospital or physician
costs have been—and those have not
been easy to control either! Hospitals and
physicians often have no alternative but
to accept Medicare’s reductions in
payments. Private plans under the new
prescription drug benefit, by contrast,
may simply exit the market if Medicare’s
reimbursement rates do not square with
drug costs and consumers’ demands.
Although private plans can attempt to
manage drug utilization, they cannot
contain costs by delaying access to care or
by narrowing the available range of
providers, techniques that are available to
HMOs. From the consumer’s perspective,
drugs offer improvements in health with
little attendant pain or inconvenience, so
new pharmaceutical innovations are
likely to draw a larger market than
comparable surgical, medical, or lifestyle
innovations. On the other hand, some
evidence suggests that new medications
reduce overall health spending. New
prescription drugs may prevent avoidable
hospitalizations and other associated
“nondrug costs,” so the use of (even
newer, expensive) medications act to
globally reduce medical spending.
29
Increases in the cost of the prescription
drug benefit beyond the original forecast
will put pressure on the entire Medicare
program and on the federal budget.
These pressures will escalate as the baby-
boom generation ages, medical
innovation continues, and problems in
the program become apparent. CMS may
feel greater pressure to hold constant or
reduce physician and hospital
reimbursement rates. The MMA
legislation incorporates temporary
increases in physician reimbursements,
extending a 1.5% increase in the fee
schedule update as opposed to a 4.5%
reduction over the next two years.
30
These increases may not be sustainable if
the prescription drug benefit proves to be
more expensive than projected or private
industry is not as eager as expected to
provide prescription drug plans in lieu of
government-administered fallback plans.
In his assessment of the MMA, Robert
Doherty, senior vice president for
governmental affairs at the American
College of Physicians, skeptically opines:
“The only certainty is that as problems
arise—and they will—[Congress] will
change the law.”
31
Impact of Medicare Reforms on
Teaching Institutions
Despite the predominance of the
prescription drug benefit, the MMA is a
hodgepodge of legislative provisions,
including several with direct impacts on
academic medicine. Teaching hospitals
constitute over 22% of the nation’s
hospitals and nearly half of its beds.
32
Typically, teaching hospitals offer service
that is broader and more technologically
advanced, care for patients who are more
acutely ill, and care that is more complex
and intensive than comparable clinical
settings.
33 The MMA legislation
incorporates several provisions— both
carrots and sticks—aimed at shifting the
paradigm of medicine from the costly
acute care paradigm of teaching hospitals
toward outpatient, preventative care.
This shift in focus complements the
MMA’s extension of Medicare insurance
to medications—the primary mode of
treatment in the outpatient setting.
Congress extended provisions within
MMA that will, in effect, reduce
reimbursement to “high-cost [academic]
programs” and will redirect resources to
the most cost-effective medical
practices.
34 On the stick side, the MMA
mandates that teaching hospitals that
receive federal support for graduate
medical education whose medical
expenditures exceed the national average
after geographically adjustments will not
get an “update,” or increase, in
reimbursement rates until FY2013.
Expected reductions in spending
stemming from these spending
“limitations” range from $500 million
over the next five years to $1.3 billion
over ten years.
35
The legislation also contained
stipulations encouraging the movement
toward care standardization, quality
improvement, and performance-based
payments.
36 Acute care hospitals must
submit data on quality measures in order
to receive a “full update” in FY2006 – 07.
If data are not submitted, CMS will
impose a 0.4 percentage point penalty
each year.
On the carrot side, from January 2004 to
2005, CMS allowed hospitals applying for
the payment of indirect and direct
medical education costs to count
residents in osteopathic and allopathic
family practice programs (in existence as
of January 2002) training at nonhospital
sites.
37 Academic institutions could then
receive support for ambulatory
training—an area of training often
neglected by a previous generation of
physicians-in-training. These and other
academic medicine-related provisions of
the MMA imply that medical education
initiatives will likely provide a net gain in
funding of about $1.9 billion over the
2004 –2013 period for most academic
medical centers.
34
These academic medicine-related
provisions of the Medicare legislation
may have some value in and of
themselves. They do not, however,
connect in any way to the MMA’s
prescription drug benefit. Increased
connections between academic medicine
and the design and implementation of
new prescription drug benefit will be
essential. Policymakers—and scholars in
medicine—should consider the efficient,
equitable, and high-quality provision of
health care services broadly, rather than
on a sector-specific basis. Academic
medicine should produce MMA-related
research that can guide in the design of
formularies and in the evaluation of the
outcomes of private plans with respect to
quality and cost of care.
Even more important, academic
medicine should turn its attention to
training the next generation of physicians
to be more effective agents and advocates
for their patients in their use of
pharmaceuticals. The prescription drug
market is unique in that an expert
physician is legally mandated to intercede
between the consumer and the producer.
The development and refinement of that
expertise lies in the domain of academic
medicine. Ultimately, the health of
seniors and the efficient use of public
funds in the new prescription drug
benefit of the MMA depend centrally on
the prescribing practices of physicians.

image_summary: 第1页：三栏文章首页，顶部为标题、作者和摘要；正文介绍MMA处方药福利、实施前老年人的药物保障状况，以及福利设计争议和“甜甜圈缺口”。
第2页：上半页左侧为术语定义框，解释CMS、双重资格者、后备计划、药品目录、Medicare Advantage、Medicaid和Medigap；其余三栏正文继续分析“甜甜圈缺口”和私人计划的作用。
第3页：三栏正文，无独立图表；讨论私人计划的药品目录、风险选择、计划过多造成的选择困难、双重资格者转换问题、参保情况及未来成本不确定性。
第4页：三栏正文，无独立图表；分析药物福利成本控制及其对医院和医师支付的压力，继而讨论教学医院、质量报告、绩效支付、门诊培训和学术医学的责任，右下开始参考文献。
第5页：三栏参考文献页，无独立图表，列出第3至第36条参考文献。
